standard.title: Particle Model of Matter
standard.description: explain observable properties of solids, liquids and gases by modelling the motion and arrangement of particles
standard.prior_knowledge: Students can classify materials as solids or liquids by observable properties and explain changes of state using heat energy (AC9S3U04). They have not yet used a particle model to explain why solids, liquids and gases behave as they do, or examined gases as a third state of matter with distinct properties.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students use a particle model — describing the arrangement, spacing and motion of particles — to explain the observable properties of solids, liquids and gases, and connect state changes to changes in particle behaviour when heat energy is added or removed.

nodes.label: Gases have observable properties distinct from solids and liquids
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can describe observable properties of gases — including that gases have mass, can be compressed, and take the shape and volume of their container — and distinguish these from the properties of solids and liquids.
nodes.minimum_width: Students describe at least two observable properties of gases and explain how these differ from the properties of solids or liquids.
nodes.typical_width: Students classify substances as solids, liquids and gases; describe the characteristic properties of each state including compressibility, fixed vs variable shape and volume; demonstrate that gases have mass; and explain what is different about gases compared with the other two states.
wider: Investigate examples demonstrating that gases have mass — using a balance to compare an empty balloon with one filled with air, or blowing air through a straw to move objects
Explore what is between gas particles — guided discussion about the nature of 'empty space' between particles and what this means for compression

Examine First Nations Australians' knowledge of gases and their applications — including the extraction of oils, medical therapies and cooking — connecting practical knowledge to particle-level understanding
nodes.hinge_reason: The empirical foundation for gas properties must precede the particle model — students who believe gases have no mass or cannot be compressed will reject the particle model explanation at Node 2 because it contradicts their existing framework. Thin treatment here produces a particle model that students apply by rote without understanding what it explains.

response_modes.reason: Students commonly believe gases have no mass ('air is nothing') and cannot be compressed ('there is nothing to compress'). Encountering multiple demonstrations of gas mass and compressibility — and discussing what is between particles — builds an accurate empirical foundation before the particle model is introduced.

success_criteria: States at least two observable properties of gases that distinguish them from solids and liquids
Provides evidence that gases have mass

nodes.label: Particle arrangement and motion explain state properties
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can use a particle model to explain the observable properties of each state — describing how particle arrangement (close/far apart) and motion (vibrating/flowing/moving freely) differ across solids, liquids and gases.
nodes.minimum_width: Students describe the particle arrangement and motion for each of the three states and connect each to at least one observable property of that state.
nodes.typical_width: Students explain all major observable properties of solids, liquids and gases using particle arrangement and motion — fixed shape (particles tightly packed, vibrating in place), liquid flow (particles close but able to move past each other), gas compression (particles far apart, moving freely) — and represent these models using diagrams or role-play.
wider: Use role-play to model particle arrangement and motion in solids, liquids and gases — examining how collective behaviour of particles produces the observable properties of each state
Observe a virtual demonstration of coloured gases being compressed and explain the change in colour intensity using the particle model — applying the model to predict observable outcomes
Explore whether there is a 'correct' way to represent particles — examining different representations (diagrams, models, animations) and what each communicates and omits
nodes.hinge_reason: The particle model as an explanatory tool is directly required for Node 3 state change explanation — students must describe particle behaviour changing during melting, evaporation and condensation. Without the model internalised as explanatory (not just diagrammatic), state change explanations collapse to observable descriptions with no particle-level reasoning.

response_modes.reason: The particle model is the first time students are asked to explain observable properties using an invisible underlying structure. The reasoning chain — particles have arrangement and motion → arrangement and motion determine macroscopic behaviour → observable properties are evidence of particle-level structure — is the scaffold that makes the model genuinely explanatory rather than decorative labelling of diagrams.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Role-play modelling and virtual compression demonstrations are genuinely effective for building the particle model concept. The representation evaluation direction connects to scientific modelling as a practice and provides substantive enrichment for advancing students.
success_criteria: Describes particle arrangement and motion for each of the three states
Uses the particle model to explain at least two observable properties — one for solids and one for gases

nodes.label: State changes are explained by changes in particle behaviour
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain state changes (melting, freezing, evaporation, condensation) using the particle model — describing how adding or removing heat energy changes particle motion and the transitions between states.
nodes.minimum_width: Students explain melting using the particle model — describing how adding heat energy increases particle motion until particles can move past each other.
nodes.typical_width: Students explain all common state changes (melting, freezing, evaporation, condensation) using the particle model, connecting heat energy addition/removal to changes in particle motion; explain why mass is conserved during state change (same particles, different arrangement); and connect this to their prior knowledge of observable state change (AC9S3U04).
wider: Examine First Nations Australians' knowledge of state changes in beeswax and resins — connecting particle-model explanation to culturally significant material use
Investigate how changes of state in materials enable recycling — explaining at the particle level why glass and metals can be returned to liquid state and reformed
Connect particle model state change to the water cycle (AC9S4U02) — explaining evaporation and condensation as particle-level processes that drive the macroscopic cycle

response_modes.reason: State change explanation using the particle model requires students to integrate observable state change knowledge (AC9S3U04), particle model knowledge, and heat energy concepts in a single explanatory account. This is the synthesis move of the descriptor — applying the model to explain a familiar phenomenon at a new level of explanation.

success_criteria: Explains at least one state change using particle arrangement and motion — describing what happens to particles when heat is added or removed
Explains why mass is conserved during a state change using the particle model
